prompt: Some people think that children should not be allowed to own a smartphone until they start secondary school. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Smartphones now reach children long before adolescence, and there is a growing view that ownership should be postponed until secondary school. I agree with this restriction, principally because primary-age children lack the self-regulation the device demands, though I would treat it as a matter of parental judgement rather than a fixed rule.

The strongest argument concerns attention. A smartphone is engineered to be difficult to put down, and an eight-year-old is being asked to resist a product designed by teams whose entire job is to make resistance fail. The consequences appear in sleep, in reading stamina and in the capacity to tolerate boredom, which is where a good deal of childhood invention comes from. Delaying ownership by three or four years does not remove the difficulty, but it postpones it until the child has more capacity to meet it.

A second argument concerns exposure. Younger children encounter material they cannot place in any context, and the social dynamics of group messaging are unforgiving at an age when friendships are already volatile. Parental controls help but are routinely circumvented.

The obvious objection is safety, and it is a genuine one: parents want to be able to reach a child walking home from school. That need, however, is met equally well by a basic handset, which provides contact without a browser or an app store. The distinction matters, because it shows the safety argument supports carrying a phone rather than owning a smartphone in particular. Parents who insist on the latter are usually solving a problem they have not named.

On balance, then, I support delaying smartphone ownership until secondary school, while accepting that the right moment depends on the individual child rather than on the school calendar.
title: Smartphones before secondary school
